readerTitle: A cooking app with 200,000 cooks and no income
caseNote: 가상 사례 (요리 앱, 식료품 체인, 쿠킹 클래스 스튜디오) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 수익 모델은 고객이 이미 하는 행동에 붙인다. 매주 반복되는 가치에는 구독을, 거래가 일어나는 순간에는 수수료를 붙인다.
misconception: 사용자가 많으면 광고를 붙이면 된다. 수익 모델은 하나만 골라야 하고, 어떤 사업에나 같은 모델이 통한다.

sources.text: 모든 수치와 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 구독 계산: 월 사용자 200,000명 × 3% = 6,000명 × $5 = 월 $30,000. 모든 수치는 가상입니다.
수수료 계산: 월 주문 10,000건 × 평균 장바구니 $60 = $600,000 × 4% = 월 $24,000. 합계 $30,000 + $24,000 = $54,000. 수수료율 4%는 가상 수치이며 실제 식료품 제휴 수수료율을 암시하지 않습니다.
쿠킹 클래스 예약 사이트의 수수료 20%는 가상 수치입니다. 실제 플랫폼의 수수료율로 읽히지 않도록 카드에 'say'로 표시했습니다.

cards.title: A cooking app with 200,000 cooks and no income
body: Maya's recipe app has 200,000 monthly users. They love it. They leave reviews like "saved my weeknights."
It earns nothing. Servers, a part-time developer and recipe testing cost her about $8,000 a month. Today you'll help her choose how to get paid, using two ways to make money from this unit.

image.label: A phone showing a recipe on a busy kitchen counter
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 부엌 조리대 위에 레시피가 뜬 휴대폰, 옆에 채소와 도마. 휴대폰 화면 구석에 빈 동전 지갑 아이콘. 실제 앱 로고나 브랜드는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Maya charge for first?
body: Her data shows a clear pattern. Most users open the app on Sunday to plan the week's dinners, then build a shopping list. Their top complaint: "Planning takes forever."

options.feedback: **Advertising** earns from every visit, but each visit pays little and needs a huge audience. Cooks with messy hands also hate tapping past ads.

options.text: A $5 monthly plan that builds a weekly menu and shopping list
options.feedback: This is a **subscription** tied to a job people already repeat every week. The value comes back each Sunday, so the payment feels earned.
Selling one item at a time is simple, but each sale starts from zero. Free recipes are everywhere, so many people won't pay for one.

cards.title: A subscription matches a weekly habit.
body: A **subscription** works when customers get value again and again, on a rhythm they can feel. Maya's users already plan every Sunday. The plan saves them an hour each time.
Say 3% of users sign up. That's 6,000 people at $5, or **$30,000 a month**. Her costs are covered, and she can see what each new feature adds to it.

cards.title: A grocery chain wants your shopping lists.
body: A regional grocery chain offers to add an "Order these ingredients" button to Maya's shopping lists. Customers would get delivery or pickup from the chain.
How should Maya get paid for it?

options.text: Take a small cut of every order placed through the button
options.feedback: A **commission** is paid only when a sale happens, by the side that gains the sale. Maya earns more as the button helps more, and users pay nothing extra.

options.text: Charge the chain a flat monthly fee to be the only grocer shown
options.feedback: Steady money, but it's no longer tied to results. Users who live far from that chain get a button they can't use.

options.text: Charge users $1 per order to use the button
options.feedback: It asks the wrong side to pay. The grocer gains the sale, yet users face a new fee and many will just shop the old way.

cards.title: Two streams, two different payers.
body: Say the button brings 10,000 orders a month, averaging $60, at a 4% cut. Subscribers pay for planning. The grocer pays for sales.
cards.callout: Each stream rides on something users already do: plan, then shop.
cards.softwareNote: This is a common shape for apps: users pay for a recurring feature, while partners pay a cut of the transactions the app sends them.

cards.title: Commissions can bend your advice.
body: If Maya earns more when baskets get bigger, she may be tempted to push recipes with pricey ingredients. Users will notice. Their trust is what the whole business runs on.

Stacking models has costs too. Adding ads to a paid plan can make subscribers feel they pay twice. And subscriptions only last while the value repeats. If weekly menus start to feel the same, people cancel.

cards.title: Now it's a cooking class studio.
body: You run a small studio in a city that teaches evening cooking classes. Most students come once, often as a gift or a date night. Few return.

options.text: Launch a monthly membership with one class a month
options.feedback: A **subscription** needs value that repeats. Most of your students come once, so few will sign up and many who do will cancel.

options.text: List classes on an experience-booking site that takes a cut, say 20%
options.feedback: A **commission** fits one-time buyers. You give up part of each ticket, but you pay only when a seat is filled.

options.text: Sell gift vouchers only on your own website
options.feedback: You keep the full price of each sale. But you must find every buyer yourself, which is slow when customers rarely come back.

cards.softwareNote: The same test works for apps: if people use it once, charge per use or per sale. If they come back weekly, a subscription can fit.

cards.title: Charge where the value already happens.
body: You used two models. **Subscriptions** fit value that repeats, like Sunday planning. **Commissions** fit a moment of sale, paid by the side that gains it. Advertising stayed a weak option because each visit paid little.
**Try it today:** write down what your customers do again and again, and where a sale happens. Next to each, note who gains and who could pay.

image.label: Two arrows: a weekly loop and a single sale
image.brief: 간단한 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 달력 위 반복 화살표 "Repeats → Subscription", 오른쪽에 장바구니와 한 번의 화살표 "Sale happens → Commission". 깔끔한 플랫 스타일.
